questions.stem: Jamie, 18, has had 4 hours of worsening generalised headache, fever, rigors, photophobia and a stiff neck. She is alert and lying flat on an ED trolley. You tell the examiner you will test for Kernig's sign. Which manoeuvre do you perform?
options: Passively flex her neck forward onto her chest and watch for her hips and knees flexing
Raise her straightened leg off the bed and note pain shooting down the back of the leg
With hip and knee flexed to 90°, passively extend the knee and note pain or resistance
Turn her head side to side two to three times a second and ask if the headache worsens
questions.why: Kernig's sign is pain or resistance (hamstring spasm) when the knee is extended with the hip flexed to 90°. It is specific but insensitive, so a negative sign does not rule out meningitis.
notes: This is Brudzinski's neck sign, the other meningeal sign examined in this station, not Kernig's.
This is the straight leg raise (Lasègue's test) for lumbosacral nerve root irritation, done with the knee kept straight.
This is jolt accentuation of headache, a separate bedside test for meningism, not Kernig's sign.

questions.stem: Jamie, 18, has had dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV in ED. At 15:10 the CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci, with culture and susceptibilities pending. She has no allergies and is not immunocompromised. What is the most appropriate change to her antimicrobial therapy now?
options: Add IV amoxicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes until the culture returns
Add IV vancomycin to ceftriaxone until pneumococcal susceptibilities are known
Switch ceftriaxone to IV benzylpenicillin because pneumococcus is the likely organism
Switch to IV meropenem alone to cover resistant Gram-positive organisms
questions.why: Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, which can be resistant to penicillin and less often to ceftriaxone. eTG says to add vancomycin to ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly until susceptibilities are known, and to keep dexamethasone going for 4 days.
notes: Listeria cover is for people over 50, pregnant women, the immunocompromised or people with alcohol dependence, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus.
Benzylpenicillin is used only as directed therapy once the isolate is shown to be penicillin-susceptible, so it is not safe while susceptibilities are pending.
Meropenem alone is not the recommended empirical regimen and does not reliably cover highly resistant pneumococci, which is the reason vancomycin is added.

questions.stem: Jamie, 18, with suspected bacterial meningitis, is given dexamethasone 10 mg IV just before her first dose of IV ceftriaxone. Why is giving dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose important?
options: It increases ceftriaxone penetration across the inflamed blood–brain barrier into CSF
It reduces CSF production by the choroid plexus, lowering pressure before the LP
It replaces cortisol lost through adrenal haemorrhage in overwhelming sepsis
It blunts the cytokine surge set off when the first antibiotic dose lyses bacteria
questions.why: Bactericidal antibiotics lyse bacteria and release cell wall components, which trigger a surge of TNF-α and IL-1 in the subarachnoid space. Giving dexamethasone first blunts this inflammation and reduces hearing loss, neurological damage and death in pneumococcal meningitis.
notes: Steroids reduce blood–brain barrier inflammation and permeability, so if anything they reduce antibiotic penetration. This is one reason vancomycin dosing needs care.
Lowering CSF production is not why it is given, and lowering pressure before the LP is not the aim of giving it early.
Adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen) is linked mainly to meningococcal sepsis, and replacing cortisol is not why dexamethasone is timed with antibiotics.

questions.stem: The ED registrar performs Jamie's lumbar puncture with her in the left lateral position. Which landmark and anatomical reason best explain the level chosen for the needle in this 18-year-old?
options: Iliac crests mark L4; L3/4 or L4/5 lies below the conus, which ends near L1–L2
Iliac crests mark L2; L2/3 lies below the conus, which ends near T12–L1
Lowest ribs mark L1; L1/2 lies below the conus, which ends near T11–T12
Posterior superior iliac spines mark L4; L5/S1 is used as the dural sac ends at L5
questions.why: In adults the spinal cord (conus medullaris) ends at about L1–L2, but the dural sac and CSF continue to about S2. The line joining the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses about L4, so the L3/4 or L4/5 space reaches CSF below the cord, where the cauda equina roots float aside.
notes: The line between the iliac crests crosses about L4, not L2, and a needle at L2/3 risks injuring the conus in some adults.
The ribs are not a lumbar puncture landmark, and L1/2 is at the level of the conus, so it risks cord injury.
The PSIS lie at about S2, and the dural sac ends at about S2, not L5, so this landmark and reason are both wrong.
